summary:
AstroPulse is a compact daily health-check device that takes about two minutes. We developed a system built around the ESP32 microcontroller, which measures heart rate and blood oxygen (MAX30102), skin temperature (DS18B20), a stress indicator (GSR), and tremor and falls (MPU6050). A color screen guides the user through each step and shows the result, LEDs and a buzzer signal warnings, and the device connects to a phone through its own Wi-Fi hotspot, so no internet is needed.

The project addresses the challenge of spotting health problems early when a doctor is far away, such as an astronaut on a space station 400 km from the nearest physician. Its key innovation is comparing each person to themselves rather than to others: the device records a personal baseline, so a heart rate of 85 bpm triggers a warning for an athlete whose normal is 60, but counts as normal for someone whose normal is 82.

Its importance extends beyond space. The same idea can protect an oil-field worker in extreme heat or an elderly person living at home. It is also a hands-on learning project that connects sensors, programming, and health in one device.
details:
AstroPulse: Project Details

1. What It Does and How It Works

AstroPulse is a daily health-check device that takes about two minutes. The user presses a button, and the color screen guides them step by step:

  1. Heart rate and oxygen: The user keeps a finger still on the MAX30102 sensor for 30 seconds. The sensor shines light into the finger and measures how much comes back. The amount changes with each heartbeat because blood surges through the finger. It uses two colors of light to tell oxygen-rich blood from oxygen-poor blood.
  2. Stress: The user places two fingers on the GSR electrodes for 20 seconds. Tiny amounts of sweat conduct electricity better, so the reading rises under stress.
  3. Temperature: The user holds the DS18B20 probe in the palm for 30 seconds.
  4. Movement: The MPU6050 is clipped to clothing the whole time and detects sudden falls and tremor.
  5. Quick phone questions: mood, hours of sleep, and symptoms.
  6. Result: The ESP32 processes the readings, compares them with the person’s own baseline, and shows the outcome:

Status

Light

Sound

Stable

Green

None

Warning

Red, slow blink

Short beep

Danger (fall or SOS)

Red, fast blink

Continuous

At any time, holding the button for 3 seconds sends an SOS. The device sends its data to a phone dashboard over a Wi-Fi network that it creates itself.

2. Benefits

  • Early detection: spots health changes before they become serious problems.
  • Works without internet: suitable for remote places.
  • Personalized: compares each person with themselves, which reduces false alarms.
  • Low cost and simple: built from common electronic parts.
  • Educational: connects students to electronics, programming, and how the body works in one project.

3. Intended Impact

  • Supporting the health of astronauts on stations far from doctors (400 km in the example).
  • Protecting workers in harsh environments, such as an oil-field worker in extreme heat.
  • Reassuring families of elderly people who live at home, through the dashboard and alerts.
  • Promoting daily self-checking and health awareness among students.

4. Tools, Hardware, Software, and Programming Languages

Hardware (from the guide):

  • ESP32 microcontroller (the brain, with built-in Wi-Fi).
  • MAX30102 for heart rate and SpO2, MPU6050 for motion, GSR for stress, DS18B20 for temperature.
  • 1.8" color TFT screen, LEDs, a buzzer, and a push button.
  • Two communication protocols: I2C (two wires, each part has an address) and SPI (faster, used by the screen), plus pull-up resistors.

Software and languages: The guide does not specify a language. The usual choice for the ESP32 is C++ in the Arduino IDE, with a phone dashboard written in web technologies (HTML/CSS/JavaScript) served by the device itself through its Wi-Fi access point. Please edit this paragraph to match what your team actually used.

5. Creative Aspects

  • Personal baseline: the smartest idea in the project. A heart rate of 85 bpm can be a warning for an athlete whose normal is 60 (+42%), yet normal for someone whose normal is 82 (+4%).
  • Combining several indicators (pulse, oxygen, temperature, stress, movement, questions) in one short check.
  • A design modeled on the human body: senses (sensors), brain (ESP32), face (screen), voice (buzzer), and hand (button).
  • Linking space to Earth: the astronaut idea becomes a solution for workers and the elderly.
  • A private Wi-Fi network that removes the need for internet.

6. Factors the Team Considered

  • Accuracy: finger movement ruins the pulse reading, so the user is asked to stay still.
  • Not relying on a single indicator: heat and exercise also raise GSR readings, so it is never used alone.
  • Skin vs. body temperature: skin (33–36 °C) reads lower than the inside of the body (≈37 °C), so readings are interpreted accordingly. The probe also needs about 30 seconds to settle.
  • Sleep: there is no sleep sensor, so the user is asked each morning instead of the device guessing.
  • Avoiding wiring mix-ups: the TFT screen is labeled SCL and SDA but actually uses SPI, not I2C, so each part’s type is checked before connecting.
  • Safety and ease of use: the GSR current is tiny and safe, the screen guides the user, and the SOS button is always available.
  • Future development: turning the device into an all-day wristband would require adding a battery, a smaller size, and likely wrist-based sensors.
